title: The Ta'iyya of al-Ilbiri
intro: This is Abu Ishaq al-Ilbiri's best-known poem, the Ta'iyya, “the poem in ta”, and al-Himyari names him by it: “the author of the ascetic ode that begins: The days crumble your heart away”. It is addressed to a man the poet calls Abu Bakr: al-Ethiopi says this was his son, while Muhammad Ridwan al-Daya, the editor of his diwan, takes him for a man who had spoken of the poet's faults and whom the poet answers with a call to knowledge and the fear of God. It opens with man's heedlessness as the days wear him away, praises knowledge above wealth, belittles the world, and calls to prayer and repentance. Then the poet gives Abu Bakr a voice to reproach him, an old man grown grey in his sins, concedes that only the least of his faults has been exposed, and returns to his counsel: shun disgrace, beware of people, leave any place of injustice, renounce the world; it ends by counting its own lines and, in some versions, with a blessing on the Prophet. It has become one of the texts students of religious learning learn by heart.

translation: The days crumble your heart away, crumb by crumb,
and the hours carve your body down, stroke by stroke.
1.sharh: The poem opens on time as a slow destroyer: the days and hours wear a man away so gradually that he does not notice.

translation: Death calls to you, and calls in earnest:
“Listen, my friend, it is you I want, you.”
2.sharh: Death's call is no idle threat, and the repeated “you” leaves no doubt whom it means.

translation: I see you love a wife who is false,
one the wise have divorced for good and all.
3.sharh: The world is a faithless wife. The wise divorce her irrevocably, as Ali ibn Abi Talib is reported to have said to the world: “I have divorced you three times, with no going back.”

translation: You sleep your whole life through, alas, snoring
in her arms, until you die, and then you wake.
4.sharh: A saying often attributed to Ali puts it the same way: “People are asleep, and when they die they wake.”

translation: How long will you be deceived, and until
how long before you turn from her? How long?
5.sharh: The repeated “until when” at the end of the line presses the question home.

translation: Abu Bakr, I have called you, if only you would answer,
to what holds your good fortune, if you have the sense:
6.sharh: Abu Bakr, named here for the first time, is the man the poem addresses; with him the call to knowledge begins.

translation: to knowledge, by which you will be a leader,
obeyed when you forbid and when you command.
7.sharh: Knowledge makes a man a leader, obeyed without wealth or rank.

translation: It clears the film from your eyes
and guides you on the way when you go astray.
8.sharh: Ignorance is a film over the eyes, and knowledge the light that clears it.

translation: In your people's gathering you wear it as a crown,
and it clothes you in beauty when you are far from home.
9.sharh: Knowledge honours its owner at home, where it is his crown, and abroad, where no one knows who he is.

translation: Its benefit reaches you as long as you live,
and its store remains for you when you are gone.
10.sharh: A hadith counts knowledge that others benefit from among the deeds whose reward goes on after death.

translation: It is the keen Indian blade that never glances off:
with it you strike whomever you strike where it kills.
11.sharh: A scholar's argument cuts like a fine sword; Indian steel made the best blades.

translation: A treasure for which you need fear no thief,
light to carry, found wherever you are.
12.sharh: Lines attributed to al-Shafi'i say the same: “My knowledge goes with me wherever I turn.”

translation: It grows the more you spend of it,
and shrinks if you close your hand on it.
13.sharh: Unlike money, knowledge grows when it is given away by teaching, and shrinks when it is hoarded.

translation: Had you once tasted its sweetness,
you would have chosen learning and striven for it,
14.sharh: Whoever turns away from learning has never tasted it.

translation: and no passion you obey would have kept you from it,
nor a world whose finery has bewitched you,
15.sharh: Once knowledge has been tasted, every distraction seems small.

translation: nor would a lovely garden have drawn you from it,
nor a curtained bower of beauties you are smitten with.
16.sharh: Neither the beauty of gardens nor the beauty of women can rival the pleasure of learning.

translation: The soul's food is the breath of meanings,
not that you have eaten and drunk.
17.sharh: Ruh, “soul”, and arwah, “breaths”, share a root: meanings refresh the soul as a breeze refreshes the body.

translation: So keep at it and take it up in earnest:
if God gives it to you, you will have it.
18.sharh: Effort is the student's part; the gift of knowledge is God's.

translation: And if you are given a long reach in it,
and people say you have outstripped them,
19.sharh: The sentence runs on into the next line: even great learning is no ground for complacency.

translation: do not feel safe from God's questioning about it,
in reproach: “You knew; did you act?”
20.sharh: A hadith says that no one's feet will move on the Day of Judgement until he is asked, among other things, what he did with his knowledge.

translation: The head of knowledge is the true fear of God,
not that it be said, “He has become a head.”
21.sharh: Ra's, “head”, and ra'asta, “you became a head”, play on each other: the head of knowledge is the fear of God, not leadership. Ibn Mas'ud is reported to have said, “The head of wisdom is the fear of God.”

translation: Let doing good be your flowing robe, not that
you be seen to have put on the robe of wrong.
22.sharh: Deeds are clothes that others see a man wearing, fine or foul.

translation: If knowledge brings you no good,
it would be better had you stayed ignorant;
23.sharh: Knowledge that does not shape conduct is worse than ignorance; the Prophet sought refuge in God from knowledge that does not benefit.

translation: and if your understanding throws you down into pits,
would that, would that you had never understood!
24.sharh: Understanding that does not guide its owner becomes a pitfall that leads him astray.

translation: From the fruits of indolence you will reap ignorance,
and grow small in people's eyes, even as you grow old.
25.sharh: Laziness is a tree whose fruit is ignorance, and no age makes up for it.

translation: If you are ignorant, you are as good as gone while you live,
and if you know, you are present though you are gone.
26.sharh: The ignorant are as good as dead while they live; the learned live on in their knowledge after they die.

translation: You will remember my words to you after a while,
and long for them when you have been kept from them;
27.sharh: He will long for this advice when it is too late to follow it.

translation: you will bite your hand in remorse for them,
and remorse avails nothing once you feel it,
28.sharh: Biting the hand in remorse is an image from the Quran (25:27): “the day when the wrongdoer will bite his hands”.

translation: when you see your companions in a sky,
risen high above you, and you sunk low.
29.sharh: The sky is a figure for the high rank that learning brings.

translation: Pay no heed to your wealth, put it out of mind:
the only wealth is what you have learned.
30.sharh: Knowledge is the only wealth that lasts; money comes and goes.

translation: The ignorant man has no worth among people,
though the kingdom of Iraq fell to him.
31.sharh: The kingdom of Iraq was proverbial for wealth and dominion.

translation: Your knowledge will speak for you in the assembly,
and be written down from you one day, if you write.
32.sharh: A scholar's words are quoted and copied long after him.

translation: What use to you is raising buildings high
if you have pulled yourself down with ignorance?
33.sharh: He builds his house and pulls himself down: the contrast is the point.

translation: You set wealth above knowledge out of ignorance:
by your life, you were not just in the case.
34.sharh: To place money above learning is itself proof of ignorance.

translation: Between the two, by the text of revelation, is a great gulf:
you will know it when you read Ta Ha.
35.sharh: Knowledge is the only thing the Prophet is told to ask God for more of.

translation: If the rich man raises the banner of wealth,
you have raised the banner of your knowledge;
36.sharh: Four lines set the rich man against the scholar, each half answering the other.

translation: if the rich man sits on cushions,
you have sat upon the stars;
37.sharh: The scholar's seat is higher than any the rich can buy.

translation: if he rides fine horses with the marks of breeding,
you have ridden the highways of piety;
38.sharh: The rich man's mount carries him to worldly ends; the scholar's carries him to God.

translation: and however many virgin beauties he deflowers,
how many virgin wisdoms you have been the first to take!
39.sharh: Thoughts no one has had before are “virgin”, and the scholar is the first to reach them.

translation: Poverty will not harm you at all
once you have come to know your Lord.
What fine reward He holds for you
when you couch your camel in the courtyard of His obedience!
41.sharh: To couch one's camel in a generous host's courtyard is to arrive as his guest; obedience brings a man to God's door.

translation: So meet my sound counsel with acceptance:
if you turn from it, you have lost;
42.sharh: Advice helps only those who take it.

translation: and if you keep it in word and deed,
and trade with God by it, you have gained.
43.sharh: Good works as trade with God is the Quran's image (35:29): “they hope for a trade that will never fail”.

translation: This world is nothing:
it grieves you for an age and gladdens you a moment;
44.sharh: The world's sorrows last for ages and its joys for moments.

translation: and its end, when you think on it,
is like your shadow, or your dream when you dream.
45.sharh: Like a shadow or a dream, the world passes and leaves nothing behind.

translation: You are imprisoned in it, and you love it:
how can you love the place where you are imprisoned?
46.sharh: A hadith calls the world “the believer's prison and the unbeliever's paradise”.

translation: It feeds you with food, and soon
it will feed on you as you fed on it.
47.sharh: The earth that fed him will feed on him in the grave.

translation: You go naked if you put on its clothes,
and are clothed if you strip off its garments.
48.sharh: To wear the world's finery is to be naked of good; to take it off is to be clothed in piety.

translation: Every day you witness a friend's burial,
as if what you witness were not meant for you.
49.sharh: He sees death come to others and never thinks it is coming for him.

translation: You were not created to settle in it, but
to cross it: so strive for what you were made for.
50.sharh: Ta'muraha and ta'buraha, “settle it” and “cross it”, differ by a single letter. A hadith says: “Be in this world as a stranger or a passer-by.”

translation: And if it falls in ruins, ruin it further yourself,
and fortify your faith as best you can.
51.sharh: Let the world crumble, and build up the faith that lasts.

translation: Do not grieve for what you miss of it
once you have won in the life to come.
52.sharh: An echo of the Quran (57:23): “so that you do not grieve over what escapes you”.

translation: What you have gained of the world is no use to you,
the perishing, if you are denied the lasting.
53.sharh: The world perishes and the hereafter lasts; only gain in the second counts.

translation: Do not laugh with fools for amusement:
you will weep, if you laugh.
54.sharh: From the Quran (9:82): “Let them laugh a little, and weep much.”

translation: How can you be glad when you are held in pledge,
not knowing whether you will be ransomed or forfeit?
55.sharh: Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned (Quran 74:38), and no one knows if he will be redeemed.

translation: Ask your Lord for success in it,
and be sincere in asking when you ask.
56.sharh: Success in this life is God's to give.

translation: When you prostrate yourself, call out to Him in confession
as Dhu al-Nun, son of Matta, called out to Him.
57.sharh: From inside the whale Jonah prayed: “There is no god but You; glory be to You; I have been one of the wrongdoers” (Quran 21:87).

translation: Keep knocking at His door; perhaps
He will open His door to you, if you knock.
58.sharh: Prayer is knocking at the door of the Generous, which opens to those who persist.

translation: Remember Him much on earth, unceasingly,
to be remembered in heaven when you remember.
59.sharh: From the Quran (2:152): “Remember Me, and I will remember you.”

translation: Do not say youth leaves room enough,
and think how many young ones you have buried.
60.sharh: Youth is no promise of time to repent later: the young die too.

translation: Now say to me: “Adviser, you need
your own advice more, if you would look with your own wits.”
61.sharh: Here the poet gives Abu Bakr a voice and lets him turn the advice back on the old man; the reply runs to line 85.

translation: “You cut me to pieces with blame for neglect,
and you have spent your whole life in neglect.”
62.sharh: Tuqatti'uni, “you cut me to pieces”, and qata'ta, “you have spent”, share a root.

translation: “In my youth you frighten me with death,
yet it never crosses your mind now you are old.”
63.sharh: The old man has more reason to fear death than the youth he lectures.

translation: “You were better guided in your youth:
what ails you, that you relapsed when you turned grey?”
64.sharh: Relapsing in old age is worse than straying in youth.

translation: “Here am I, who have not waded the sea of sins
as you waded it, until you drowned;”
65.sharh: Sin is a sea that drowns those who wade in.

translation: “I have not drunk the heady wine of the world,
and you drank it until you were drunk;”
66.sharh: Love of the world is a wine that leaves the drinker senseless.

translation: “I have not camped in a valley of injustice,
and you camped there and poured yourself into it;”
67.sharh: He did not merely stop in the valley of injustice; he flowed into it like water.

translation: “I did not grow up in an age of profit,
and you grew up in one and did not profit.”
68.sharh: The poet grew up in an age rich in learning and scholars, and did not benefit.

translation: “You kept company with great scholars,
and I never saw you follow those you kept company with.”
69.sharh: Keeping company with scholars is useless without following their example.

translation: “The Book called to you, and you did not answer;
grey hair checked you, and you did not wake.”
70.sharh: The Quran called him and grey hair warned him, and he heeded neither.

translation: “Playing the boy is ugly in a youth,
and uglier still an old man playing the young.”
71.sharh: What is forgiven in youth is not forgiven in age.

translation: “So you deserve reproach more than I,
and if wrongdoers held their peace, you would not have spoken.”
72.sharh: If wrongdoers kept the silence that becomes them, the poet, being one, would never have spoken.

translation: “Blame yourself; blame no one else
for a fault: your own self is the fittest to blame.”
73.sharh: A man should look to his own faults before anyone else's.

translation: “Were your eyes to weep blood in fear
for your sin, I would not tell you you are safe.”
74.sharh: No weeping could match the weight of his sins.

translation: “And who will make you safe, when you are a servant
commanded, who neither heeded nor obeyed?”
75.sharh: A disobedient servant has no claim to safety from his master.

translation: “You are weighed down with sins, and do not fear,
in your ignorance, being found light when you are weighed.”
76.sharh: From the Quran (101:8–9): “As for him whose scales are light, his mother is the Pit.”

translation: “You pity the man who persists in sin,
and show him mercy, and to yourself you show none.”
77.sharh: He sees sin in others and not in himself.

translation: “You have gone backwards and stumbled blindly:
by your life, had you arrived, you would not have turned back.”
78.sharh: Had he truly reached the right path, he would never have left it.

translation: “Had you met your Lord without a sin,
and had He gone through your account in full, you would have perished;”
79.sharh: A hadith: “Whoever's account is examined closely will be punished.” Only God's forgiveness saves.

translation: “nor would He wrong you in any deed, but
it is hard to carry out what you were charged with.”
80.sharh: God wrongs no one; the fault lies in failing to carry the trust.

translation: “Had you come on the Day of Decision alone,
and seen the dwellings there, so far apart,”
81.sharh: From the Quran (19:95): “Each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.” The sentence is completed in the next line.

translation: “you would have felt the greatest remorse there, in anguish
for all you have wasted in your life.”
82.sharh: On that day remorse comes too late.

translation: “You flee the midday heat and shield yourself from it:
why have you not fled from Hell?”
83.sharh: He shelters from the summer sun and does nothing to shelter from Hell.

translation: “You could not bear its lightest torment:
were you made of iron, you would melt in it.”
84.sharh: A hadith says the lightest punishment in Hell is that of a man with two embers under his feet that make his brain boil.

translation: “Do not be deceived: the matter is in earnest,
and not as you reckoned or supposed.”
85.sharh: With this warning Abu Bakr's reply ends.

translation: Abu Bakr, you have exposed the least of my faults,
and covered most of them, and the worst.
86.sharh: The poet answers in his own voice and concedes: the truth is worse than Abu Bakr said.

translation: Say whatever shameful things you like of me,
and double them: you have spoken the truth.
87.sharh: He accepts every charge and more, in earnest, not in irony.

translation: However you fault me, I know so well
what is in me that it is as if you had praised me.
88.sharh: Knowing his own heart, he finds any criticism mild.

translation: Do not consent to faults: they are a great
disgrace that earns a man hatred,
89.sharh: The poet resumes his counsel to Abu Bakr.

translation: and bring the man of standing down from the Pleiades,
and give him the bottom in place of the top;
90.sharh: Faults bring down even the highest, and no rank protects a man they have stained.

translation: just as acts of obedience shoe you with the bright stars
and bring you near, though you are far away,
91.sharh: Obedience raises a man so high that the stars are his sandals.

translation: and spread fine report of you in the world,
so you meet kindness in it wherever you are,
92.sharh: Good deeds win a good name and kindness everywhere.

translation: and walk its broad paths in honour,
and reap praise from what you have planted.
93.sharh: “Its broad paths” (manakib) is the Quran's word for the tracts of the earth (67:15).

translation: Now you are known for no blemish,
nor have you stained your robe since you grew up,
94.sharh: Abu Bakr's record is still clean, and the poet urges him to keep it so.

translation: nor raced in the field of falsehood,
nor spurred on in it, nor trotted;
95.sharh: Falsehood is a racecourse, and Abu Bakr has not yet run in it.

translation: but if you do not keep far from it, you will be caught in it,
and who can free you once you are caught?
96.sharh: It is easier to keep away from falsehood than to get free of it.

translation: It will stain what was pure in you, until
it is as if you had never been pure,
and you become the prisoner of your sin, in bonds:
how can you be freed, once you are taken?
Fear your fellow men and beware of them
as you fear lions and leopards.
99.sharh: People can do more harm than wild beasts, and less openly.

translation: Mix with them, and keep apart from them, wary,
and be like the Samaritan when you are touched.
100.sharh: Mix with people, but be ready to pull back from them as if touch were forbidden.

translation: If they are insolent to you, say “Peace”:
perhaps you will be safe, if you do.
101.sharh: From the Quran (25:63): “When the ignorant address them, they say: Peace.”

translation: But who can promise you safety in an age
that reaches the mountain goats, unless you are protected?
102.sharh: Even the goats on the highest peaks are hunted down; no one is safe but those whom God protects. Al-usm, “the mountain goats”, and usimta, “you are protected”, share a root: even the creatures that take refuge on the heights find none.

translation: Do not linger with a people where injustice
kills the heart, unless you are in chains.
103.sharh: Injustice kills the heart: leave, unless you cannot.

translation: Go west: the stranger finds a market;
go east, if you are choking on your spittle.
104.sharh: Leave: a stranger is in demand abroad like goods at market, and travel relieves distress. Gharrib, “go west”, chimes with gharib, “stranger”, and sharriq, “go east”, with shariqta, “you choked”; together they mean simply “travel”.

translation: Renouncing the world is no obscurity:
you are its prince when you renounce it;
105.sharh: To need nothing from the world is true sovereignty.

translation: and if there were any above the prince in it,
in height and in glory, it would be you.
If you scatter it and leave it
for the Abode of Peace, you are safe;
107.sharh: Dar al-salam and salimta, “the Abode of Peace” and “you are safe”, share a root.

translation: and if you honour it and look on it
with reverence, you have degraded yourself.
108.sharh: To honour the world is to degrade oneself.

translation: I have gathered counsels for you; follow them
all your life: they are the best you could follow.
109.sharh: The counsel ends here, and the poet turns to the poem itself.

translation: I have drawn out my reproach, and added to it,
because you have drawn out your idleness.
110.sharh: The length of the reproach matches the length of the idleness.

translation: Do not hold my failings and lapses against me,
but take my counsel to you, if you are wise.
111.sharh: Take the advice, whatever the failings of the one who gives it.

translation: I have added six fine lines to it,
and before that it was a hundred and six.
112.sharh: The poem counts itself: a hundred and six lines, with six more added later.

translation: And bless, my Lord, the last of the messengers,
and his noble family, as long as You are remembered.
113.sharh: The poem ends, as many do, with a blessing on the Prophet and his family, for as long as God is remembered, that is, for ever.

3.1.3.head: عِرس
3.1.3.meaning: Irs: a man's wife; here, the world.

6.1.1-2.meaning: Abu Bakr: the kunya of the man the poem addresses. Who he was is uncertain: al-Daya guesses Abu Bakr ibn al-Hajj, and al-Ethiopi says the poet's son.

8.1.5.head: غَشا
8.1.5.meaning: Ghasha: a film over the eye. Al-Daya's edition has asha, “weak sight”.

9.1.4.head: نادي
9.1.4.meaning: Nadi: the assembly where one's people gather.

11.2.3.head: مَقاتِل
11.2.3.meaning: Maqatil: the vital spots, where a blow kills.

16.2.2.meaning: Khidr: a curtain screening a girl's quarters.

16.2.3.head: رَبرَب
16.2.3.meaning: Rabrab: a herd of wild cows, the old Arabic image for a group of beautiful women.

17.1.3.head: أَرواح
17.1.3.meaning: Arwah: breezes, refreshment; plural of rawh.

19.1.4-5.meaning: Tul ba': a long reach; ability, mastery.

22.1.1.head: ضافٍ
22.1.1.meaning: Dafi: long and flowing, of a garment.

24.1.5.meaning: Mahawin: pits, places one falls into.

35.2.3.meaning: Ta Ha: Sura 20, which has the verse “Say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge” (20:114).

38.1.4.head: مُسَوَّمَة
38.1.4.meaning: Musawwamat: marked, as fine horses were.

39.1.4.head: غانِيَة
39.1.4.meaning: Ghawani: beautiful women; plural of ghaniya, one who needs no adornment.

41.2.4.head: أَناخَ
41.2.4.meaning: Anakhta: you made your camel kneel, alighting as a guest.

44.2.2.head: حِقبَة
44.2.2.meaning: Hiqba: a long stretch of time.

45.2.1.head: فَيء
45.2.1.meaning: Fay': the afternoon shade that falls where the sun was, and moves on.

55.1.5.head: رَهن
55.1.5.meaning: Rahn: a pledge, held as security for a debt.

55.2.5.head: غَلِقَ
55.2.5.meaning: Ghaliqta: you are forfeit, as a pledge is when the debt goes unpaid.

57.2.3-4.meaning: Dhu al-Nun: “the man of the fish”, the prophet Jonah (Yunus).

57.2.6.meaning: Matta: the name Muslim tradition gives Jonah's father.

64.2.6.head: نُكِسَ
64.2.6.meaning: Nukista: you relapsed, as a patient falls ill again.

66.1.3.meaning: Humayya: the strength of wine, its first heady rush.

66.1.4-5.meaning: Umm Dafr: “mother of stench”, a name for the world.

67.2.4.head: اِنهَمَلَ
67.2.4.meaning: Inhamalta: you poured out, as tears do.

70.2.1.head: نَهنَهَ
70.2.1.meaning: Nahnahaka: checked you, held you back.

78.1.3-4.meaning: Khabatta ashwa: you stumbled like a night-blind she-camel; a proverb for going forward without sight.

79.2.1.head: ناقَشَ
79.2.1.meaning: Naqashaka: examined you closely, letting nothing pass.

81.1.4-5.meaning: Yawm al-fasl: the Day of Decision, the Day of Judgement.

83.1.3.meaning: Al-hajir: the midday heat of summer.

88.2.1.head: باطِنَة
88.2.1.meaning: Batina: one's inner self, what is hidden.

90.1.4.meaning: Al-Thurayya: the Pleiades, proverbial for height.

91.1.3.head: نَعَلَ
91.1.3.meaning: Tan'aluka: makes into sandals for you.

93.1.3.head: مَناكِب
93.1.3.meaning: Manakib: the broad tracts and paths of the earth.

95.2.2.head: أَوضَعَ
95.2.2.meaning: Awda'ta: you spurred on; properly of camels urged to speed.

95.2.5.head: خَبَّ
95.2.5.meaning: Khababta: you trotted; khabab is a fast gait.

99.2.4.head: سَبَنتى
99.2.4.meaning: Al-sabanta: the leopard; any bold beast of prey.

100.2.2.head: السّامِرِيّ
100.2.2.meaning: Al-Samiri: the Samaritan who made the golden calf for the Israelites, punished never to touch anyone or be touched (Quran 20:97).

101.1.2.head: جَهِلَ
101.1.2.meaning: Jahilu 'alayka: “they were ignorant towards you”: they were insolent; jahl here is rashness, not want of knowledge.

102.2.2.head: أَعصَم
102.2.2.meaning: Al-usm: mountain goats with white on their forelegs, which live on the peaks.

104.1.4.meaning: Nafaq: being in demand, of goods; a ready market.

104.2.5.head: شَرِقَ
104.2.5.meaning: Shariqta: you choked; to choke on one's spittle is to be in distress.

107.2.2-3.meaning: Dar al-salam: the Abode of Peace, Paradise.

112.1.3.meaning: Sittan: six. Al-Ethiopi's text has “nine”, which makes his 115 lines.

113.1.3-4.meaning: Tamam al-rusul: “the completion of the messengers”, the Prophet, the last of them.
